
<!-- slide 205 -->
# Synteny & Rearrangements {.divider}

[Comparing whole genomes · plotsr]{.eyebrow}


<!-- slide 206 -->
## What plotsr Draws {.smaller}

[plotsr · theory]{.eyebrow}

### Synteny and structural rearrangements across assemblies

[plotsr](https://github.com/schneebergerlab/plotsr) visualises how several chromosome-level assemblies line up: long **syntenic** blocks (same order, same strand) plus the **rearrangements** between them, inversions, translocations, duplications. Each genome is a horizontal track; ribbons connect homologous regions between adjacent genomes.

It doesn't compute the comparison itself. It consumes the structural annotation from **SyRI**, so the pipeline is always: align the genomes, find rearrangements with SyRI, then plot with plotsr. Reach for it when you have two or more good assemblies and want to *show* their differences, not tabulate them.


<!-- slide 207 -->
## Step 0 — Install {.smaller}

[plotsr · install]{.eyebrow}

### Bioconda is the easy path

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
plotsr ships on bioconda, which pulls the pinned NumPy / pandas / matplotlib it needs. A fresh environment keeps it isolated.

```bash {code-line-numbers="1-2|4"}
# one clean environment
conda create -n synteny -c bioconda plotsr
conda activate synteny

plotsr -h            # confirm it's on PATH
```

If you install from source instead, plotsr pins **Python < 3.12** and **NumPy < 2**, build the env accordingly.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```bash
$ plotsr -h
usage: plotsr --sr SR --genomes GENOMES -o OUT
  --sr        SyRI output (repeat per pair)
  --genomes   genomes information file
  --tracks    feature tracks (genes, SNPs…)
  --markers   labelled markers (BED)
  --cfg       visual config
  --reg / --chr   zoom to region / chrom
  --itx       cross-genome (itx) mode
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 208 -->
## Where the Input Comes From {.smaller}

[plotsr · upstream]{.eyebrow}

### Align → SyRI → plotsr

To compare genomes `A → B → C`, you align each adjacent pair and run SyRI on each. This is the data-generation step; plotsr only reads the result.

```bash {code-line-numbers="1-4|6-8"}
# 1) whole-genome alignment with minimap2 (asm5 for same-species)
minimap2 -ax asm5 --eqx A.fa B.fa | samtools sort -O BAM - > A_B.bam
samtools index A_B.bam

# 2) structural annotation with SyRI  → A_Bsyri.out
syri -c A_B.bam -r A.fa -q B.fa -F B --prefix A_B
```

Each `*syri.out` lists every syntenic block and rearrangement between one pair, exactly what plotsr stacks.


<!-- slide 209 -->
## Step 1 — The Example Data {.smaller}

[plotsr · data]{.eyebrow}

### Four *Arabidopsis* accessions, ready to plot

The repo ships a complete example: Col-0, Ler, Cvi, Eri. Grab it and you have all inputs without running an alignment.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```bash {code-line-numbers="1-2|4-7"}
git clone https://github.com/schneebergerlab/plotsr.git
cd plotsr/example

ls
# genomes.txt
# *.chrlen              (chrom lengths)
# col_lersyri.filtered.out
# ler_cvisyri.filtered.out
# cvi_erisyri.filtered.out
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
The three `*syri.filtered.out` files are the pairwise comparisons (Col↔Ler, Ler↔Cvi, Cvi↔Eri); the order of the genomes is the order they'll stack.
:::
::::


<!-- slide 210 -->
## Step 2 — `genomes.txt` {.smaller}

[plotsr · data]{.eyebrow}

### One line per genome, in stacking order

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Each row is a genome: a length source, a display name, and style tags. `ft:cl` means the file is a **chromosome-length table** (faster than parsing a FASTA).

```bash
$ cat genomes.txt
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```text
#file                  name   tags
TAIR10_Filtered.chrlen col-0  ft:cl;lw:1.5
ler.chrlen             ler    ft:cl;lw:1.5
cvi.chrlen             cvi    ft:cl;lw:1.5
eri.chrlen             eri    ft:cl;lw:1.5
```

A `.chrlen` is just two columns:
```text
Chr1   30427671
Chr2   19698289
Chr3   23459830
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 211 -->
## Step 3 — The SyRI Annotation {.smaller}

[plotsr · data]{.eyebrow}

### Each row is one block, tagged by type

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
The columns are reference coords, query coords, an ID, its parent block, and the **annotation type**. plotsr colours by that type.

```bash
$ head -5 col_lersyri.filtered.out
```

Types it draws: `SYN` (syntenic), `INV` (inversion), `TRANS` (translocation), `DUP` (duplication), `NOTAL` (not aligned).
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```text
Chr1  1       1084     - -  -     -        -       NOTAL1  -    NOTAL
Chr1  1085    1771083  - -  Chr1  1        1773924 SYN1    -    SYN
Chr1  1085    158550   - -  Chr1  1        157500  SYNAL1  SYN1 SYNAL
Chr1  158551  158596   - -  Chr1  157501   157556  HDR1    SYN1 HDR
Chr1  158597  270144   - -  Chr1  157557   269099  SYNAL2  SYN1 SYNAL
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 212 -->
## Step 4 — The Minimal Plot {.smaller}

[plotsr · build]{.eyebrow}

### Three comparisons, one genomes file

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Pass one `--sr` per pairwise comparison, plus `--genomes`, and name an output. plotsr stacks the four accessions and draws every block.

```bash {code-line-numbers="2-4|5-6"}
plotsr \
  --sr col_lersyri.filtered.out \
  --sr ler_cvisyri.filtered.out \
  --sr cvi_erisyri.filtered.out \
  --genomes genomes.txt \
  -o output_plot.png
```

Grey is syntenic; orange/green/blue mark the rearrangements.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![](images/plotsr_min.png){width="100%"}
:::
::::


<!-- slide 213 -->
## Step 5 — Add Feature Tracks {.smaller}

[plotsr · build]{.eyebrow}

### Layer gene density, SNPs, centromeres

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
`--tracks tracks.txt` adds annotation lanes above the genomes. Each line in the file is a GFF/BED/bedGraph with its own style tags (bin width, colours, label).

```bash {code-line-numbers="6"}
plotsr \
  --sr col_lersyri.filtered.out \
  --sr ler_cvisyri.filtered.out \
  --sr cvi_erisyri.filtered.out \
  --genomes genomes.txt \
  --tracks tracks.txt \
  -o output_plot.png
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```text
$ cat tracks.txt
TAIR10_GFF3_genes.gff  Genes  ft:gff;bw:10000;...
1001genomes.snps.bed   SNPs   bw:10000;lc:sienna;...
Giraut2011_cents.bed   Centromeres  bc:palegreen;...
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 214 -->
## Step 6 — Markers, Config, Sizing {.smaller}

[plotsr · build]{.eyebrow}

### The publication figure

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
`--markers` labels specific loci, `--cfg` tunes legend/colours, and `-S -W -H -f` set syntenic-ribbon spread, width, height, and font size.

```bash {code-line-numbers="7-8|9"}
plotsr \
  --sr col_lersyri.filtered.out \
  --sr ler_cvisyri.filtered.out \
  --sr cvi_erisyri.filtered.out \
  --genomes genomes.txt \
  --tracks tracks.txt \
  --markers markers.bed \
  --cfg base.cfg \
  -o output_plot.png -S 0.5 -W 7 -H 10 -f 8
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![](images/plotsr_full.png){width="100%"}
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
plotsr is a pipeline endpoint: **align → SyRI → plot**. Feed it one `--sr` per pair and a `genomes.txt`, then layer `--tracks` and `--markers` for the final figure. Grey is conserved order; colour is everything that moved.
:::


<!-- slide 215 -->
## Exercise · Your Turn {.smaller}

[plotsr · exercise]{.eyebrow}

### Zoom and switch modes

::: {.exercise}
[Command-line exercise]{.xl}
Starting from the full command, (1) zoom into the inversion-rich region of chromosome 3, then (2) redraw the whole thing in cross-genome (`--itx`) mode.

```bash
# 1) zoom a single region (note: --reg alone, not with --chr)
plotsr ... --cfg base.cfg --reg col-0:Chr3:6600000-10000000 -o zoom.png

# 2) itx mode — chromosomes drawn end-to-end across genomes
plotsr ... --cfg base.cfg --itx -S 0.7 -o itx.png
```

Which mode makes the Chr4 inversion easier to see, and why?
:::
